pieces.text: In 1908, Austria-Hungary took control of territories known as Bosnia and Herzegovina. Many people in these territories and the nearby country of Serbia were angry. They believed Bosnia and Herzegovina should be controlled by
people, or members of an ethnic group that spoke Slavic languages such as Serbian or Russian.

textContent.text: Many nationalist groups formed hoping to free Bosnia and Herzegovina from foreign rule. Young Bosnia was one of these groups. One of its members was Gavrillo Princip, a 19-year-old from a Serbian family. On June 28, 1914, while Archduke Francis Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary was visiting Bosnia, Princip shot and killed both the archduke and his wife.

The royal couple's murder infuriated Austria-Hungary. With Germany's support, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia. This assassination proved to be a nationalistic "spark" that helped to ignited the flames of war across Europe.

textContent.text: In 1914, a Serbian nationalist assassinated a top official from Austria-Hungary. Austria-Hungary responded by declaring war on Serbia, sparking a chain reaction that forced allies to declare war. Although Serbia wasn't an official member of an alliance, it had strong ties to Russia. So, Russia immediately stepped in to defend Serbia. Then, Germany supported its ally Austria-Hungary by declaring war on Russia. Next, France joined the war to uphold alliance agreements with Russia. This made Great Britain join with the Allied powers to defend both France and Russia.

contents.text: Airplanes and submarines were modern industrial weapons used for the first time in World War I. They provided strategic advantages that land-based weapons could not. Read the information below. Then follow the instructions.

mainText.text: At the start of the war, airplanes were used to take photos of the enemy's position. As the war went on, planes were updated to carry weapons. By 1915, planes could fly in, hidden by the clouds, and drop bombs or shoot enemy targets with machine guns. In 1916, air-to-air combat emerged with enemy planes fighting each other in the air.

World War I submarines could stay underwater for hours, gathering information on the location of the enemy. Submarines also carried bombs called torpedoes to attack enemy ships. Most importantly, submarines moved quietly and were rarely detected. So, enemies were in constant fear of surprise attacks.
